blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: Define globalisation, and identify what it involves for trade, for companies and for the movement of people and information.

blocks.heading: Globalisation, defined
blocks.text: Globalisation is the growing integration of the economies of the world. Goods, services, finance, information and people move between countries more widely than before, and companies spread their production and their sales across several countries at once. The word names a process rather than a single event: the ties tend to grow a little closer each year, and each shock travels a little further.

blocks.heading: One bottle, four countries
blocks.text: Kaoko Juice presses marula fruit at Opuwo. In a year it sells 12 000 bottles through Namibian shops and exports 4 000 bottles to Botswana. The glass bottles come from a works in Germany and the labels from a printer in Portugal. One small firm, one bottle, four countries: trade across borders, a company buying and selling in several of them at once, and production split between them. A learner meets the same picture in any shop in Oshakati - rice from Vietnam on the shelf beside mahangu from the fields outside town.

blocks.heading: What it includes
blocks.text: When a question asks what globalisation involves, four features answer it: goods and services produced in one country and sold in others; companies with operations in more than one country; information and finance moving worldwide; and people travelling, studying and working across borders. The four travel together, because a firm that sells abroad tends to move money, people and know-how across the same borders.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The specialisation of topic 6.1 explains why these cross-border ties pay: each country does more of what it makes best. The exchange rates of topic 6.3 price the trade that results, and the firms that carry much of it are the subject of the next section.
